title: Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity -- Ch. 23: Basher v. Comelec: Resolving "Insignificant Cases"
keywords: Barangay Maidan, Tugaya, Lanao del Sur
notice of the time, place and purpose
primary_topics: Chapter 23 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' -- CJP's account of Basher v. Comelec, an apparently 'insignificant' barangay election case that the Supreme Court took up anyway because it could not let an injustice pass.

His four-fold demonstration that the disputed August 30, 1997 'election' in Barangay Maidan was illegal, irregular and void: the situs, the voting time, the election date and the manner of postponement were all outside what the law allows.

The notice holding: an abbreviated announcement 'over the mosque' minutes before a nine o'clock evening voting was not sufficient notice and should in fact be equated with 'no notice,' following and extending Hassan v. Comelec.

His larger point about the Court's role: even small cases get full attention once the Court sees the need to correct an injustice and to lay down jurisprudential teachings that will guide lower tribunals and future elections.
sub_topics: He recalls his own earlier observation in Chapter 1 that cases over a few hundred pesos, an ejectment, an illegal dismissal, a slander or a barangay chairman's election protest sometimes reach the Supreme Court.

The facts: Basher and Ampatua both ran for punong barangay in Maidan, Tugaya, Lanao del Sur; the May 12, 1997 election failed, the June 12 special election failed, and the exercise was reset to August 30, 1997.

The Comelec's version: voting began only around 9:00 p.m. because of tension, after religious leaders warned the election officer that it 'might trigger bloodshed,' the mayor yelled and threatened her, and armed followers pointed guns at her and her military escorts.
The tally showed Ampatua 250 votes, Basher 15 and a third candidate 10, and Ampatua was proclaimed winner.

Basher's petition: no election was held at the place and time prescribed by law; the candidates had agreed that no election would be held, the ballot box was turned over to the PNP for safekeeping, and the voting was conducted that night at the residence of the former mayor without any announcement.

The case's internal history: originally assigned to Justice Sabino R. De Leon Jr., who would have affirmed the Comelec, until CJP dissented during deliberations and the Court sided with him 11-2, converting his Dissent into the ponencia.

First ground -- an illegal situs: Section 42 of the Omnibus Election Code requires a public school or public building within the barangay, and the election appears to have been held at a former mayor's house in another barangay, while Cagayan Elementary School was the validly designated voting center; to that date no respondent had disclosed where the voting actually occurred.

Second ground -- irregular voting time: the law and Comelec Resolution 2971 fix voting from 7:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., and the exception for voters already waiting within thirty meters presupposes an election that commenced on time and merely continues.

His warning that the Comelec's strained reading encourages clandestine elections at midnight and discourages suffrage by exposing voters to the dangers of the dead of night in far-flung barangays threatened by rebel and military gunfire.

Third ground -- an invalid date: Section 2 of RA 6679 governs suspension or postponement, and only the Comelec, not an election officer, has authority to declare a failure of election, even with the candidates' agreement.

Fourth ground -- invalid postponement: Datu-Imam's own report shows she held no proceeding, summary or otherwise, to determine whether any legal ground existed, having declared a verbal failure of election 'just to ease their aggression.'

Fifth and most significant ground -- irregular notice: the electorate was not told of the exact schedule and venue; announcing the election over the mosque minutes before voting could not let the electorate know of the activity or choose discerningly not to take part.

Hassan v. Comelec applied: if one day's notice was held 'too short' there, the much shorter notice here should all the more be declared wanting, since the time for holding an election 'must be authoritatively designated in advance.'

Justice De Leon's Dissent: the mosque announcement sufficed in a small, predominantly Muslim barangay, there was no adequate proof that the voting occurred at the former mayor's house, the Court is not a trier of facts, and courts should be slow in nullifying elections absent proof of the statutory conditions for a failure of election.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 23 of 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity' takes up Basher v. Comelec, which some would call an insignificant case, to show that the Supreme Court takes up such matters anyway when it cannot let an injustice pass. Hadji Rasul Batador Basher and Abulkair Ampatua contested the post of punong barangay in Maidan, Tugaya, Lanao del Sur; after two failed elections the exercise was reset to August 30, 1997, but according to the Comelec voting began only around nine that evening amid tension, threats from the town mayor and guns drawn between his followers and the election officer's military escorts. Ampatua was proclaimed with 250 votes to Basher's 15. Basher alleged that the candidates had agreed there would be no election, that the ballot box had been turned over to the police, and that the voting was later conducted at the former mayor's residence without announcement. The case was assigned to Justice Sabino R. De Leon Jr., who would have affirmed the Comelec, but CJP dissented during deliberations, the Court sided with him 11-2, and his Dissent became the ponencia. It held the exercise void on four grounds and a fifth that he called most significant. The situs was illegal, since Section 42 of the Omnibus Election Code requires a public building within the barangay and the designated Cagayan Elementary School was not used. The time was irregular, since voting runs from seven in the morning to three in the afternoon and the thirty-meter exception presupposes an election already begun. The date and the postponement were invalid, since only the Comelec may declare a failure of election and the election officer held no summary proceeding. Finally, the announcement over the mosque minutes before voting was no notice at all, a conclusion drawn a fortiori from Hassan v. Comelec. Justice De Leon dissented, urging deference to the Comelec's findings and caution in nullifying elections.
